passage:
Dear Rajni Masi,

You asked why I have gone quiet on the phone. The truth is that some kids in my class call me weird, poor, and other things about my body. They do it when the teacher isn't looking, and sometimes they copy how I talk. Last week someone stuck a note on my bag. I cried in the washroom and hated myself for a while. But I have been thinking: nothing they say is my fault. Their words are about them. I've started spending lunch in the art room, where nobody cares what I wear. Yesterday I showed the note to my class teacher, and she said she would deal with it. I wanted you to know, so that I'm not alone in this.

Love,
Jasleen

qa.q: Where has Jasleen started spending lunch?
How did Jasleen feel at first, and how has Jasleen's thinking changed?
qa.a: Jasleen first felt hurt and ashamed, crying in the washroom, but now believes the mocking is not Jasleen's fault and that the bullies' words are about them.

qa.q: What did Jasleen do that helps in this situation?
qa.a: Jasleen protected their self-respect by not believing the bullies' story, found a place to fit in at the art room, and reported the harassment by showing the note to the class teacher.

qa.q: How might Rajni Masi feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Probably sad and protective, but also proud that Jasleen spoke up. She asked why Jasleen had gone quiet, so she cares and will be glad to know.

grounding: The protagonist is mocked, refuses to believe the story, finds a place to fit in and reports the harassment.
